terms.gloss: a certain, a particular (one not named); some
terms.grammar: pronoun and adjective; quiddam as a noun
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.104: lūdendī etiam est quīdam modus retinendus
terms.comment: It also softens a word: timiditāte ingenuā quādam, with a sort of well-bred shyness (Cic. de Or. 2.10).

evidence: Cic. Brut. 64: habet certōs suī studiōsōs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: sometimes used like quīdam, of things or people that exist but are not named.

phrases.latin: lūdendī etiam est quīdam modus retinendus
phrases.english: even in play a certain limit must be kept

phrases.latin: bene quīdam dīxit dē amīcō suō, 'dīmidium animae suae'
phrases.english: someone put it well, calling his friend “half of his soul”
One day he thought to himself

sources: Lewis & Short: quidam · Lewis & Short: certus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 86, 288.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-augustinus, loci-quintilianus), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations of Cicero’s De oratore (Wilkins) that are not in the loci collections were checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 9 November 2026. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word.
